explanations.answer: If Jesus is the One who was to come
explanations.explanation: John sends two of his disciples with one question, and it's a big one. He wants to know, "Are You the One who was to come, or should we look for someone else?" No small talk, no warm-up. I wish my questions were that tidy, because mine show up with a ten-minute introduction.

explanations.answer: If Jesus will come and baptize with him
explanations.explanation: That's a fair guess, since John the Baptist is known for baptizing. But the text never has John ask for that. He sends two men to ask whether Jesus is "…the One who was to come…" or whether they should look for someone else.

explanations.answer: If Jesus will teach them how to pray
explanations.explanation: Nothing about prayer lessons here, friend. John's messengers carry one question, and it's about who Jesus is. They ask if He is "…the One who was to come…" or if they should look for someone else. That's the whole errand.

Yes. The passage says that at that very hour Jesus healed many people of their diseases, afflictions and evil spirits. He also gave sight to many who were blind. John's men show up with a question, and that's the hour this is happening. That's like asking if the bakery is open while you're smelling cookies from the sidewalk.

The text says the opposite. At that very hour Jesus healed many people of their diseases, afflictions and evil spirits. He also gave sight to many who were blind. So when John's men arrive, Jesus is already at work, and they get to see it.

explanations.answer: What they have seen and heard
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, "Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard…" He doesn't give a plain yes or no. He sends them back with what's right in front of them. Those two just watched Jesus heal people, so they're carrying an eyewitness report.

explanations.answer: That John should come and see
explanations.explanation: Jesus never invites John to come in this passage. He tells the two men to "…report to John what you have seen and heard…" The men are the ones who saw, so they're the ones who carry the news back.

explanations.answer: That they must wait for a sign
explanations.explanation: No waiting here, friend. Jesus doesn't tell them to hold off for anything. He says, "Go back and report to John what you have seen and heard…" They've already seen plenty, since Jesus healed many people at that very hour.

The poor, yes. Jesus ends His list with "…and the good news is preached to the poor." It comes right after the blind, the lame, the lepers, the deaf and the dead. It's the last item, and it's easy to rush past.
Priests aren't on this list. Jesus says "…the good news is preached to the poor." The text names the poor, and that's the answer here. Priests just aren't in the verse.
No kings on this list, friend. Jesus says "…the good news is preached to the poor." The poor are who the text names. That's the word that fits the blank.

explanations.answer: The one who does not fall away because of Him
explanations.explanation: Right. Jesus says, "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me." That's the last thing He says to John's messengers. John asked a question, and Jesus answers with what they've seen and then this blessing.

explanations.answer: The one who has seen His miracles up close
explanations.explanation: Close, because the messengers did just see healings. But the blessing isn't about that. Jesus says, "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me." It's about not falling away on account of Him.

explanations.answer: The one who keeps every word of the law
explanations.explanation: That isn't the blessing Jesus gives here. He says, "Blessed is the one who does not fall away on account of Me." The blessing is about not falling away on account of Him. Keeping the law doesn't come up in that line.

The text says something different. Jesus says, "Look, those who wear elegant clothing and live in luxury are found in palaces." So if the crowds wanted a man in fine clothes, the wilderness was the wrong place to look. I own a tall white hat, and even I wouldn't wear it out to the desert.

Right, false. Jesus says, "Look, those who wear elegant clothing and live in luxury are found in palaces." Palaces, not the wilderness. His point is that the crowds didn't go out there to see a man in fine clothes.

explanations.answer: Yes and more than a prophet
explanations.explanation: That's what Jesus says. He answers His own question: "A prophet? Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet." John is a prophet, and Jesus says he is more than that. It's a big answer to a simple question.

explanations.answer: No he is only a teacher
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't say that. When He asks if they went out to see a prophet, He answers, "Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet." He doesn't make John smaller. He makes him bigger.

explanations.answer: Not yet but someday he will be
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't put it off. He says plainly, "Yes, I tell you, and more than a prophet." That's about John right now, with no "someday" in it.

Yes, prepare. Jesus quotes, "Behold, I will send My messenger ahead of You, who will prepare Your way before You." The messenger goes first and gets the way ready. That's the job Jesus says is written about John.
Guarding the way sounds like a good job. But the Scripture Jesus quotes says the messenger "…will prepare Your way before You." So the job is preparing.
Finding a way is a good job too, but it's not the one in the verse. Jesus quotes that the messenger "…will prepare Your way before You." The way gets prepared, and that's the whole assignment.

The text says the opposite of that. Jesus says, "…yet even the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he." That comes right after He says no one born of women is greater than John. So the least in the kingdom of God is greater than John.
Right, false. Jesus says no one born of women is greater than John. Then He adds, "…yet even the least in the kingdom of God is greater than he." Read it slowly, because it's a lot to take in.

That's the reason the passage gives: "For they had received the baptism of John." The tax collectors are named on purpose. Even they acknowledged God's justice, and the text ties it to John's baptism.

explanations.answer: They had paid back what they owed
explanations.explanation: The text doesn't say anything like that. The reason it gives is, "For they had received the baptism of John." That's what it ties to their acknowledging God's justice.

explanations.answer: They had given money to the poor
explanations.explanation: That's a kind thing to do, but it isn't the reason in this passage. The text says they acknowledged God's justice, "For they had received the baptism of John." The reason is the baptism.

Yes. The text says the Pharisees and experts in the law "…rejected God’s purpose for themselves, because they had not been baptized by John." That sits right next to the people who received John's baptism and acknowledged God's justice. It's the opposite response.

The text says the opposite of that. The Pharisees and experts in the law "…rejected God’s purpose for themselves, because they had not been baptized by John." The people who had received John's baptism, even the tax collectors, acknowledged God's justice. So welcoming it isn't what the Pharisees and experts in the law do.
The text doesn't show them asking John anything. It says they "…rejected God’s purpose for themselves, because they had not been baptized by John." So the answer is rejecting it.

explanations.answer: The others did not dance or weep
explanations.explanation: Yes. The children call out, "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep." They played a happy tune and a sad one, and they didn't get the response they wanted either way. That's a tough crowd.

Nobody's fighting about volume in this picture. The children say, "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep." Their complaint is that the others didn't dance or weep.

explanations.answer: The others took their flute away
explanations.explanation: No flute thieves in this story, friend. The children say, "We played the flute for you, and you did not dance; we sang a dirge, and you did not weep." Their complaint is about what the others did not do. The others did not dance and did not weep.
That's right. John came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and Jesus says people respond, "He has a demon!" Faultfinding is what Jesus describes. John came one way and still got criticized.
No praise here, friend. Jesus says John came neither eating bread nor drinking wine, and the people said, "He has a demon!" That's faultfinding, not a pat on the back.

explanations.answer: They bring him bread and wine
explanations.explanation: Bread and wine come up, but only as what John didn't have. He came "…neither eating bread nor drinking wine…" The people's response, according to Jesus, is "He has a demon!"

The text says it didn't go that way. Jesus says that when the Son of Man came eating and drinking, people said, "Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" So He didn't get approval, just a different complaint. John came one way, Jesus came another, and both got criticized.

Right, false. Jesus says the Son of Man came eating and drinking, and people said, "Look at this glutton and drunkard, a friend of tax collectors and sinners!" That isn't approval. It's the same crowd with a new complaint.
Yes, right. Jesus says, "But wisdom is vindicated by all her children." Vindicated means proven right. It's His closing line after both John and the Son of Man got criticized.
That word flips what Jesus says. His line is, "But wisdom is vindicated by all her children." Vindicated means proven right, so the sentence goes the other direction.
Not weak, friend. Jesus says, "But wisdom is vindicated by all her children." Vindicated means proven right. The line has nothing to do with weakness.
